title: Gravitational Acceleration
short_intro: Gravitational acceleration is the acceleration experienced by a body due to the gravitational force exerted by a massive astronomical body. It acts radially towards the center of mass of the source body under standard central-field conditions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Variation of g with altitude, depth, and latitude, along with basic pendulum and free-fall problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Non-inertial reference frames, centrifugal force effects due to Earth's rotation, spheroidal earth geometry, and interior density models.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Surface Value
bullets: Defined as the force per unit mass experienced by a test particle in a gravitational field: g = F/m.
At the surface of a spherically symmetric Earth of mass M and radius R, g = GM/R<sup>2</sup>.
Dimensionally expressed as [L T<sup>-2</sup>] with SI units of m s<sup>-2</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Variation with Altitude (Height)
bullets: As height h above the surface increases, the effective gravitational acceleration decreases as g(h) = GM/(R+h)<sup>2</sup>.
For small heights (h << R), the binomial approximation yields g(h) ≈ g(1 - 2h/R).
The fractional change in gravitational acceleration is twice the fractional change in height for h << R.

concept_notes.heading: Variation with Depth
bullets: Assuming a uniform density sphere, the mass contributing to the gravitational pull at depth d is only the inner sphere of radius (R - d).
The acceleration at depth d is given by g(d) = g(1 - d/R).
Gravitational acceleration decreases linearly with depth and vanishes identically at the exact center of the Earth (d = R).

concept_notes.heading: Variation with Latitude (Rotation of Earth)
bullets: Earth's rotation about its polar axis introduces a non-inertial centripetal/centrifugal correction to the measured gravity.
The effective gravity at latitude λ is g' = g - Rω<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup>λ, where ω is the angular velocity of Earth.
Gravity is maximum at the poles (λ = 90°) and minimum at the equator (λ = 0°).

derivations.title: Variation of g with Altitude
derivations.conditions: Spherical Earth of mass M, radius R, height h above surface
steps: Write the general expression for gravitational acceleration at distance r = R + h from the center: g(h) = GM / (R + h)<sup>2</sup>.
Factor out R from the denominator: g(h) = GM / [R<sup>2</sup>(1 + h/R)<sup>2</sup>] = g / (1 + h/R)<sup>2</sup>, noting that g = GM/R<sup>2</sup>.
Use the binomial expansion for h << R: (1 + h/R)<sup>-2</sup> ≈ 1 - 2h/R.
Substitute back to obtain the approximate variation: g(h) ≈ g(1 - 2h/R).

derivations.title: Variation of g with Depth
derivations.conditions: Uniform density sphere of mass M, radius R, depth d below surface
steps: Express the uniform density of Earth as ρ = M / [(4/3)πR<sup>3</sup>].
The effective mass enclosed within radius r = R - d is M' = (4/3)π(R - d)<sup>3</sup> ρ.
Substitute ρ into M' to get M' = M (R - d)<sup>3</sup> / R<sup>3</sup>.
Calculate g(d) = G M' / (R - d)<sup>2</sup> = G [M (R - d)<sup>3</sup> / R<sup>3</sup>] / (R - d)<sup>2</sup> = (GM/R<sup>2</sup>) * (R - d)/R.
Simplify using g = GM/R<sup>2</sup> to obtain g(d) = g(1 - d/R).

graphs_and_experiments.title: g versus Distance r from Earth Center
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A continuous graph with r on the x-axis and g on the y-axis. Inside the Earth (r < R), a straight line starting from origin to g at r=R. Outside the Earth (r > R), a curved hyperbola falling as 1/r^2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows linear increase inside the earth transitioning smoothly to an inverse-square decrease outside the surface, peaking precisely at r = R.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in objective questions asking to identify the correct qualitative variation of g across the boundary r = R.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Compound Pendulum Experiment for g
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bar pendulum oscillating about a horizontal axis with adjustable knife edges, measuring time period T versus distance l from center of mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Allows accurate experimental determination of local acceleration due to gravity using the relation g = 4π<sup>2</sup> / slope of T<sup>2</sup> vs L graph.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Standard laboratory technique conceptualized in theoretical viva and conceptual viva questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Barometric or Kater's Pendulum Configuration
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Graphical representation of reversible pendulum time periods showing intersection of curves for equal periods.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Eliminates radius of gyration errors to determine absolute local value of g.

solved_numericals.question: At what height above the Earth's surface is the value of gravitational acceleration reduced to 36% of its value at the surface?
solution_steps: Let surface gravity be g and gravity at height h be g_h = 0.36 g.
Use the relation g_h = GM/(R + h)<sup>2</sup> and g = GM/R<sup>2</sup> to set up the ratio: g_h / g = R<sup>2</sup> / (R + h)<sup>2</sup>.
Take the square root on both sides: 0.6 = R / (R + h).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the percentage change in the value of acceleration due to gravity for a body taken to a depth of 64 km inside the Earth. Take Earth's radius R = 6400 km.
solution_steps: Use the depth variation formula: g(d) = g(1 - d/R).
Fractional change in g is given by (g - g(d))/g = d/R.
Substitute the given values: d = 64 km, R = 6400 km.

solved_numericals.question: At what latitude will the effective acceleration due to gravity become zero due to the Earth's rotation? (Assume R = 6400 km and angular speed ω = 7.29 × 10<sup>-5</sup> rad/s).
solution_steps: The effective gravity formula considering rotation is g' = g - Rω<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup>λ.
Set g' = 0 to find the condition: 0 = g - Rω<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup>λ.
Rearrange to solve for cosλ: cos<sup>2</sup>λ = g / (Rω<sup>2</sup>).
Substitute standard values: g ≈ 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>, R = 6.4 × 10<sup>6</sup> m, ω = 7.29 × 10<sup>-5</sup> rad/s.
Since g ≈ 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> is much larger than Rω<sup>2</sup> ≈ 0.034 m/s<sup>2</sup>, cos<sup>2</sup>λ = 9.8 / 0.034 > 1, which is physically impossible.
Conclude that Earth's current rotation rate is insufficient to make effective gravity zero at any real latitude (it would require an angular speed about 17 times faster).
solved_numericals.answer: Not possible at any latitude with current rotation speed (cos^2(lambda) > 1)

assumptions_and_limitations: Earth is assumed to be a spherically symmetric body with concentric shells of uniform density for elementary derivations.
Binomial approximations are valid strictly when the altitude h is much smaller than the Earth's radius R.
Centrifugal force calculations treat the Earth as a rigid body rotating at a constant angular velocity about a fixed geometric axis.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gravitational acceleration is strictly constant everywhere on the Earth's surface.
common_misconceptions.correct: It varies with latitude due to Earth's rotation and equatorial bulge.
common_misconceptions.why: Earth is an oblate spheroid (flattened at poles) and rotates, making centrifugal force and distance from center latitude-dependent.

common_misconceptions.wrong: g is maximum at the center of the Earth.
common_misconceptions.correct: g is zero at the exact center of the Earth.
common_misconceptions.why: At the center, mass surrounding the point exerts symmetric gravitational pulls in all directions that cancel out completely.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Altitude formula g(h) = g(1 - 2h/R) can be used for any arbitrary height.
common_misconceptions.correct: It is an approximation valid only when h << R.
common_misconceptions.why: Higher-order terms in the binomial expansion become significant when h is comparable to R.

quick_revision: g decreases with altitude as g(1 - 2h/R) for h << R.
g decreases linearly with depth as g(1 - d/R).
g is maximum at poles and minimum at the equator due to Earth's rotation.
